newsitem.title: USA: Sexual harrassment - little boys, big corporations.
newsitem.headline: Sexual harrassment - little boys, big corporations.

text.p: The newest face of sexual harassment, five years after the U.S. Senate hearings that forced it into public consiousness, is a bright-eyed little boy, a symbol of apparent political correctness run amok.

But feminists say real progress has been made since law professor Anita Hill accused Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas of sexual harassment in 1991, notably by opening a useful debate on the issue.
In the last two weeks, pre-pubescent boys in North Carolina and New York drew headlines by kissing female classmates and getting suspended from school on the grounds of sexual harassment.

Red-faced officials in Lexington, North Carolina, and the New York City borough of Queens retrenched when the cameras started to roll, but the issue of sexual harassment has extended from an Illinois auto plant to the U.S. military to the White House since being brought to prominence by the Thomas hearings.
"I think the impact has been very positive overall, and long-term," Patricia Ireland, president of the National Organisation for Women, said in an interview.

Even the publicity accorded the young "harassers" is a measure of how far the issue has come, Ireland said: "Whenever we make a great deal of progress, somehow someone makes a story to try to exploit and trivialise the issue."

The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which tracks charges of sexual harassment -- and ironically was the agency where both Thomas and Hill worked when that alleged harassment occurred -- shows the annual number of charges filed more than doubled since 1991 to 15,549 in 1995.

In one celebrated case, the EEOC has charged Mitsubishi Motor Manufacturing of America with "creating a hostile and abusive work environment" at its plant in Normal, Illinois, alleging women were groped, grabbed, touched and forced out of their jobs if they complained.

Even when complaints bypass the EEOC, they often make news. The most visible case in point is the sexual harassment suit filed by former Arkansas state worker Paula Jones against President Bill Clinton. The case is proceeding, even though Clinton's lawyers want it postponed until he leaves office.
At the Defence Department, new rules and training have cut down on incidents of sexual harassment of women in the military, but the Pentagon acknowledges it remains a major problem.
A majority of military women, or 55 percent, reported getting unwanted sexual attention at work over the previous 12 months in 1995. That was down from 64 percent in 1988.
The real inroads may have been made in the American psyche, according to Karlyn Bowman, an expert on polling at the American Enterprise Institute.

Before the televised hearings that eventually resulted in Thomas's confirmation to the Supreme Court, polls of American public opinion never asked about sexual harassment, Bowman said. But studies since show wide agreement on what does or does not constitute sexual harassment, he said.
After the hearings, Bowman said, "People's attention was focused again on the women's movement ... Raising the issue of sexual harassment caused people to think about the issues in a different way."
But sexual harassment was the issue women worried about least, Bowman said, far behind concern about losing a job, balancing work and family and not being valued by an employer.

Leslie Wolfe, president of the Washington-based Centre for Women Policy Studies, was encouraged by the fact that major corporations were beginning to take prevention of sexual harassment "quite seriously as a corporate responsibility."
"The important thing is for the institution to change, for men and women somehow to have equal partnerships and respectful relationships in the workplace," Wolfe said.
